title: C++: references, pointers and copies

authoring.author: Parikshaa content team
authoring.originality: Written for Parikshaa: our own lesson text and examples on c++: references, pointers and copies, examples, code, quiz and explanations; no text from any site, book or course.

outcomes: can predict whether a function changes its caller's variable
can choose between value, reference, const reference and pointer parameters
can explain why large objects are passed by const reference

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.body: In C++ the way you write a parameter decides two things at once: whether the function can change the caller's data, and whether the data gets copied. Getting it wrong gives either a bug (a change that silently does nothing) or a slow program (a vector of a million names copied on every call). Placement tests ask "what does this print?" about exactly this, and code reviewers flag it on sight.

sections.heading: Three ways to pass
sections.body:
- **By value** (`int marks`): the function gets its **own copy**. Changes stay inside the function.
- **By reference** (`int& marks`): the parameter is **another name for the caller's variable**. Changes are the caller's changes. The call looks like a normal call: `addBonus(b)`.
- **By pointer** (`int* marks`): the function gets the **address** and must dereference it (`*marks += 5`). The caller writes `&c`, so the possible change is visible at the call site, and the pointer may be `nullptr`, which the function must check.

A reference must be bound when it is created and **can never be re-seated** to refer to something else; `alias = 100` assigns to `b`, it does not make `alias` refer to 100. A pointer can be changed to point elsewhere, or to nothing.

> **Note:** A useful default: **references for "must be there", pointers for "may be absent".** If a function cannot work without the object, take a reference; if `nullptr` is a meaningful input, take a pointer.

sections.heading: Which ones change the caller?
sections.body: All three functions add a bonus of 5. Only two of them reach the caller's variable.

code.expected_output:
value: 70, reference: 75, pointer: 75
b after alias = 100: 100
code.caption: Value, reference and pointer parameters

sections.heading: const references: no copy, no change
sections.body:
Passing a `vector<string>` or a big struct **by value** copies every element on every call. For a read-only function that is pure waste. The fix is a **const reference**: `const Roster& r`. The function sees the caller's object directly (no copy), and the `const` means the compiler rejects any attempt to modify it.

The rule of thumb used in most C++ codebases:

| Parameter type | Read only | Will modify |
|---|---|---|
| small (int, double, char, pointer) | by value | by reference |
| large (string, vector, struct) | by **const reference** | by reference |

Small types are cheaper to copy than to reach through an address, so they stay by value.

sections.heading: Counting the copies
sections.body: `Roster` counts how many times it is copied. Two calls by value copy it twice; two calls by const reference copy nothing.

code.caption: Pass by value copies; pass by const reference does not

sections.heading: The dangling reference
Common mix-ups
sections.body:
**Many students think a reference is a pointer with nicer syntax.** It is implemented with an address, but the rules differ: a reference cannot be null, cannot be re-seated, and needs no `*` to use. Treat it as a second name, not as a variable holding an address.

**Many students think `const` slows code down.** It has no runtime cost. It is a promise the compiler checks, and it lets callers pass temporaries: `countByConstRef(Roster{})` works, but a non-const reference cannot bind to a temporary.

**Many students think passing by value is always safer.** It is safer against accidental changes, but `const&` gives the same safety without the copy.

sections.heading: Interview questions
sections.body: Answers as a strong candidate would say them.

qa.a: A reference is an alias that must be initialised, cannot be null and cannot be re-seated; you use it like the object itself. A pointer holds an address, can be null, can be re-pointed, and needs dereferencing. I use references when the object must exist and pointers when absence is meaningful.

qa.q: Why pass a vector by const reference?
qa.a: Passing by value copies every element on each call, which is O(n) time and memory for nothing if the function only reads. A const reference avoids the copy and the const stops the function from modifying the caller's vector.

qa.q: What is wrong with returning a reference to a local variable?
qa.a: The local is destroyed when the function returns, so the reference dangles and using it is undefined behaviour. Return by value instead; the compiler moves or elides the copy.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
- By value copies; by reference aliases; by pointer passes an address that may be null.
- A reference can never be null or re-seated.
- Large read-only arguments: `const T&`. Small ones: by value.
- Never return a reference or pointer to a local.
- References for "must exist", pointers for "may be absent".

quiz.stem: `void f(int x) { x = 9; }` is called as `f(a)` with `a = 1`. What is `a` afterwards?
quiz.explanation: x is a copy; the caller's a is untouched.

quiz.stem: `int a = 1, b = 2; int& r = a; r = b; r = 7;` What are a and b?
quiz.explanation: r always names a; r = b copies 2 into a, then r = 7 sets a to 7. b is never touched.

quiz.stem: Best parameter for a function that only reads a `vector<string>` of 10^6 names?
quiz.explanation: No copy, and const prevents accidental changes.
Only a pointer can be null; references always refer to an object.

hands_on.title: Put a pair in order
hands_on.task: Read `t`, then `t` lines with two integers. Fill in `orderPair(int& lo, int& hi)` so that afterwards `lo` holds the smaller value and `hi` the larger. The program prints each pair after the call.

revision_card.front: C++ parameters: value vs reference vs pointer, and the default for big read-only objects?
revision_card.back: Value copies; reference is an alias (never null, never re-seated); pointer is an address that may be null. Big read-only args: const T&. Never return a reference to a local.
